title: Is Progress 8 Relevant in 2022?
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles, drawing on a past career as a tax inspector, argues that school leaders and teachers defensively dismiss Progress 8 data when they should be using it to judge their own school, department and class. He contends that the measure is more robust than staff assume, showing that dropping English literature for one class would cut whole-school Progress 8 by only about 0.03. Breaking the data down by attendance in a school he supports reveals a very different story: pupils with 95 percent attendance or better score around +0.8, while the rest of the year group pulls the overall figure to zero. The lesson is that asking what story the data tells can show that the curriculum and teaching are working when pupils attend. He concludes that most improvement effort should therefore go into raising attendance rather than chasing other gaps.
points: Educators often discredit performance data over a single legitimate weakness, which Salles ties to fear of accountability and Ofsted.
He recommends using Progress 8 internally to judge a school, department or class rather than leaving interpretation to external bodies.
Cutting a class's English literature entry would lower whole-school Progress 8 by only about 0.03, so the measure is less fragile than critics claim.
Splitting Progress 8 by attendance showed +0.8 for pupils attending over 95 percent, revealing that the curriculum adds value when pupils are present.
His practical conclusion is that around 80 percent of improvement effort in such a school should go to raising attendance.
quotes: In my four years no one ever tried to go to court, where the man in the street would judge them. They always negotiated a settlement. The data always told a more plausible story.
But, not so. You run some maths and find that the whole school Progress 8 will only be reduced by about -0.03. You can live with that.

Now, imagine that your school isn’t full of middle class students who all had supportive, educated parents and space and resources to study during the pandemic. You will expect a negative Progress 8 this year, or at best a 0.00.
But now, let’s look at Progress 8 by attendance. Then we find a totally different picture. Students with 95% + attendance have a Progress 8 of +0.8.
That now tells the story of your curriculum. When students attend, your curriculum adds significant value.
And here’s the thing. None of those worries are the main problem. None of that is going to make a difference.
